sentences: Venus, goddess of love, born from sea foam, drifts ashore on a giant scallop shell.
Wind arrives from the left and land from the right to greet her.
Take a moment first to see the whole scene.
Sandro Botticelli of Florence most likely painted it around 1484 to 1486.
For a long time it was thought that a member of the Medici family commissioned it, but scholars now doubt that story.
Today it hangs in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence.
At upper left, Zephyr, the west wind, puffs out his cheeks and blows her toward the shore.
The woman wrapped around him is read as Aura, a gentle breeze, or as Chloris, his wife.
Tangled together in flight, the pair seem to be the wind itself.
Pink roses tumble on the breeze around the two winds.
Scholars point to verses by the Florentine poet Poliziano, in which Zephyr makes the flowers bloom.
Pick one rose and follow its path as it drifts down on the wind.
Now come closer to her face and neck.
The neck is impossibly long, and her left shoulder slopes strangely, melting into the arm.
Botticelli chose flowing, graceful line over anatomical accuracy.
Look closely at her windblown hair and you will find traces of gold.
Botticelli added gold highlights not only to the hair, but to wings, fabrics and even the shell.
The gilded strands ripple like living waves.
She covers herself with both hands, a modest pose borrowed from ancient sculpture.
Yet so much weight falls on her left leg that she could hardly stand.
The historian Kenneth Clark put it well: she is not standing but floating.
On the right shore, a goddess of the seasons, probably Spring, rushes forward with a flowered cloak.
Her white dress is scattered with small blue flowers.
The painter stops time just before the cloak reaches Venus.
The paint is tempera, pigment bound with egg, laid on two pieces of canvas sewn together rather than on a wooden panel.
Canvas was the cheaper support, and it was becoming popular for secular pictures in country villas.
At a time when most large paintings were Christian, devoting a canvas this size to a pagan nude from mythology was a bold choice.
The first writer to mention it was Giorgio Vasari, who saw it at the Medici villa at Castello.
Before you move on, step back and see whether wind, waves, hair and cloth all flow in the same direction.
Perhaps what Botticelli painted is less a single moment than one long, graceful movement.
